summary: Chloroquine phosphate is a 4-aminoquinoline antimalarial and amebicidal agent used to treat and prevent malaria caused by susceptible Plasmodium strains and to treat extraintestinal amebiasis. Doses are expressed as chloroquine base; each 500 mg phosphate tablet equals 300 mg base. It is ineffective against chloroquine-resistant strains (widespread in P. falciparum) and against the hypnozoite liver stages of P. vivax/P. ovale, which require an added 8-aminoquinoline. Major safety concerns are irreversible retinopathy with prolonged/high-dose use, fatal cardiotoxicity (cardiomyopathy, QT prolongation, arrhythmias), severe hypoglycemia, and hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. As little as 1 g can be fatal in a child.
indications: Treatment of uncomplicated malaria due to susceptible P. falciparum, P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. vivax
Prophylaxis of malaria in geographic areas where chloroquine resistance is not present
Limitation: not for complicated malaria, not for prophylaxis where resistance occurs, does not prevent P. vivax/P. ovale relapse

moa: Chloroquine, a 4-aminoquinoline, is an antiprotozoal agent whose precise mechanism is not known. Against Plasmodium it is thought to concentrate in the acid vesicles of the parasite and inhibit polymerization of heme; it may also inhibit certain enzymes through interaction with DNA. It is active against erythrocytic forms of susceptible Plasmodium species and against trophozoites of Entamoeba histolytica in vitro, but not against gametocytes or exoerythrocytic (hypnozoite) forms.

absolute: Presence of retinal or visual field changes of any etiology (for indications other than acute malaria)
relative: Cardiac disease, history of ventricular arrhythmias, uncorrected hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, bradycardia <50 bpm
monitor: Concomitant drugs with retinal toxicity (e.g., tamoxifen)
Long-term therapy (eye, muscle/nerve, renal, hematologic monitoring)

preg: In animal studies embryo-fetal developmental toxicity (including ocular malformations) occurred at 3 to 16 times the maximum recommended therapeutic dose. In humans, observational data and a meta-analysis at recommended antimalarial doses have shown no increase in birth defects or spontaneous abortion. Review the individual benefit-risk balance before prescribing in pregnancy.
lact: Chloroquine and its metabolite desethylchloroquine are excreted in breast milk; following a single 600 mg base dose the maximum daily amount an infant could receive was about 0.7% of the maternal dose. This is inadequate to protect the infant, so separate chemoprophylaxis is required. Weigh benefit to mother against potential serious adverse reactions in the infant.
renal: Chloroquine is substantially excreted by the kidney; the risk of toxic reactions may be greater with impaired renal function. Use care in dose selection in the elderly and monitor renal function. Subnormal glomerular filtration is a significant risk factor for retinopathy. Proteinuria with reduced GFR (phospholipidosis) has been reported; discontinue if renal toxicity is suspected.
hepatic: Chloroquine concentrates in the liver, so it should be used with caution in patients with hepatic disease or alcoholism or with other known hepatotoxic drugs. Hepatitis and increased liver enzymes have been reported.

major: QT-prolonging/arrhythmogenic drugs (e.g., amiodarone, moxifloxacin) - increased ventricular arrhythmia risk
Cyclosporine - sudden increase in serum cyclosporine; monitor levels, discontinue chloroquine if needed
Cimetidine - inhibits chloroquine metabolism, raising plasma levels; avoid concomitant use
Tamoxifen and other retinotoxic drugs - not recommended together
moderate: Insulin and other antidiabetic drugs - enhanced hypoglycemic effect; may need dose reduction
Ampicillin - reduced bioavailability; separate by at least 2 hours
minor: Antacids and kaolin - reduce chloroquine absorption; separate by at least 4 hours
Intradermal human diploid-cell rabies vaccine - reduced antibody response at prophylactic doses
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce gastrointestinal upset.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; alcoholism increases hepatic concentration and hepatotoxicity risk.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause ECG changes (T-wave inversion/depression, QRS widening, QT prolongation) and may lower blood glucose.

common: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, anorexia
serious: Irreversible retinopathy/maculopathy with visual field defects
rare: Neuropsychiatric changes (psychosis, delirium, depression, suicidal behavior)
emergency: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation (may be fatal)
Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS

monitoring: Baseline ophthalmologic exam within first year (BCVA, automated 10-degree visual field, SD-OCT); annual exams if risk factors, otherwise after 5 years
ECG and serum potassium/magnesium in patients with cardiac risk or on QT-prolonging drugs
Periodic complete blood counts during prolonged therapy
Blood glucose if symptoms suggestive of hypoglycemia
Periodic assessment of muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes on long-term therapy
Renal function in elderly and impaired patients

pk: Symptom relief within minutes to hours; toxic effects can appear within minutes
Prophylaxis dosed once weekly; deposits in tissues for prolonged periods

pearls: Always express and check the dose as chloroquine base: 500 mg phosphate = 300 mg base

Does not eradicate P. vivax/P. ovale hypnozoites; add an 8-aminoquinoline to prevent relapse
Retinopathy risk rises with daily dose >2.3 mg/kg, use >5 years, renal impairment, and concurrent tamoxifen
In patients of Asian descent retinal toxicity may appear outside the macula; test the central 24 degrees
As little as 1 g can be fatal in a child - overdose is a life-threatening emergency
missed: For weekly malaria prophylaxis, take the missed dose as soon as remembered, then resume the regular weekly schedule. For treatment courses, follow the prescriber's instructions; do not double a dose to make up for a missed one given the narrow margin between therapeutic and toxic doses.
overdose: Chloroquine overdose is a life-threatening emergency; toxic symptoms (nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, visual disturbance, cardiovascular collapse, convulsions, hypokalemia, QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, ventricular arrhythmias) can occur within minutes and may progress to fatal respiratory and cardiac arrest. Treatment is symptomatic and prompt: immediate gastric evacuation (emesis or lavage) then activated charcoal, with cardio-respiratory and hemodynamic support, potassium monitoring, and management of arrhythmias and convulsions.
